extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners and examiners (prosecutors, attorneys, agents)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for drafting claims and specifications and for prosecuting or defending patents to survive or overcome §101 subject-matter eligibility rejections, drawn from Federal Circuit case law summaries and practice takeaways.

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful framing of 'need' and background
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid broad need statements in the background that characterize the invention in overly general terms (e.g., 'the idea of network-controlled charging stations').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe the specific problem being solved (for example, needing to program each charging station individually, leading to inflexibility and extra work) rather than making broad, high-level need statements; an overly broad background can be used to invalidate the patent under broad claim interpretations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid claims that merely 'collect and compare known information'
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that perform only collecting and comparing known information, without requiring a step based on the comparison, are often found ineligible under §101.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If possible, draft claims to perform a step based on the comparison or to include additional, concrete actions (e.g., immunization step in Classen) so the claim does something with the comparison; emphasize any post-comparison action to support eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim a specific improvement in computing-device capabilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims should be directed to a specific improvement in computing devices (a specific manner of performing a function) rather than to an abstract idea with computers used as generic tools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Articulate claims with enough specificity at Alice step one to show they are not directed to an abstract idea; focus on how particular claim elements provide a technical improvement (e.g., a specific manner of displaying a limited set of information) rather than only claiming a desirable result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclose technical problems in the specification and how the invention solves them
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification should describe technical problems in prior user interfaces (or other computer systems) and explain how the claimed invention solves those problems with improved technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claim the structure and/or process for the improvement, not just the result. Be specific about how particular claim elements improve functioning of the computer system (examples: saving user navigation steps, improving usability on small screens).

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide specification detail showing improvement of computer functionality
rubrics_metrics.description: When arguing improvement of a computer's ability to function to overcome §101, the specification must contain more detail than generic descriptions of computer components or their inherent abilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include specific structural or inventive improvements (not merely 'reserve memory for advertising' or other generic hardware recitations). If an argument for improved computer function is needed, support it with concrete, technical disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish from business-method/abstract-data-collection claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that obtain and compare intangible business-related data (e.g., credit-card transaction parameters) and do nothing with the comparison are typically characterized as business methods or abstract ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argue that the claims describe a technical solution to a technical problem rather than a business method; point out how the claim does something technical (not merely data gathering or business logic). Use factual distinctions to show the claim is not analogous to limited precedents like CyberSource.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not claim data structures alone—tie data to tangible use
rubrics_metrics.description: Data structures or profiles (e.g., a device profile) by themselves are not necessarily statutory; claiming only data may be treated as non-tangible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claim use of the profile (a method or device that uses the profile) or claim a tangible, non-transitory medium storing the data structure. Ensure a claim uses the data to solve a technical problem rather than merely existing as data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid claiming only information-based results without inventive means
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that define a desirable information-based result (collecting, analyzing, and displaying information) in general terms, without limiting inventive means of achieving the result, are likely to fail §101.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include inventive technological elements or specific means for performing the functions; do not leave the claim as a high-level goal. Emphasize particular technical mechanisms that perform the collection/analysis/display in a non-conventional way.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterize technical problem/solution in technical terms and include non-business examples
rubrics_metrics.description: When drafting/specifying, characterize the problem and solution in technical infrastructure terms and provide examples that are not solely business-related.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid focusing exclusively on the business problem; include examples that show how the claimed invention addresses a technical issue in computer networks or systems (e.g., integration of data across sites, navigation in 3D spreadsheets). This helps analogize to favorable cases (Enfish, Core Wireless, DDR).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prosecution and argument strategies to oppose §101 rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple tactics can be used to challenge examiner §101 rejections and unfavorable characterizations of claims as abstract ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strategies include: attack the identification of the abstract idea (ensure the rejection is tied to the case facts and avoid language taken out of context); argue claims recite a technical solution to a technical problem; point to generation of new information (analogy to Enfish); emphasize user interactivity and improved data presentation (analogy to Core Wireless); point to a particular inventive technological process (distinguish from Electric Power); use guidance/memos (McRo, Enfish, Berkheimer) and training materials; argue that the examiner's broad/simplified characterization (collect/analyze/display) is unreasonable; and press for a narrower, claim-specific abstraction in the §101 analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Challenge broadest reasonable interpretation and oversimplification
rubrics_metrics.description: Argue that the examiner's or court's characterization of a claim as an overly broad abstraction (e.g., 'collecting information, analyzing it, and displaying certain results') is unreasonable and improperly removes claim detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate how claim elements provide more than the caricature used to compare the claim to abstract-idea cases; show that Enfish, McRo, DDR, etc., were decided on specific claim-level improvements and that similar specifics exist in your claims.
